Section 01
As-Is Process — Current State
How banking fraud investigation works today
Current State

Traditional fraud detection relies on static, rule-based systems with manual analyst review. Each alert goes through a sequential human process that is slow, inconsistent, and generates high false positives.

1. Rule Engine — Transaction Stream Ingestion
Static thresholds fire alerts (e.g., transaction > ₹2,00,000). Alert generated and added to queue. 200+ alerts/day with only 3 analysts.
2. Fraud Investigator — Manual Review (45–90 min)
Pull Transaction (Core Banking) → Check Customer (CRM + KYC) → Review Device (IP/Geo logs) → Check Watchlists (AML/Sanctions). 6–8 disconnected systems.
3. Analyst Investigation
Analyst manually checks 6–8 disconnected systems — core banking, CRM + KYC, IP/geo logs, AML/sanctions watchlists — copy-pasting between screens.
4. Compliance Officer — Regulatory Review
AML/KYC/PMLA check → Prepare STR/SAR if required by policy. 15% of STR filing deadlines missed.
5. Senior Manager — Approve or Block
Final escalation for approval authority. Outcome: Approve or Block & Report. 35% false positive rate causes customer friction and wasted effort.
✕ High false positive rate (~35%) — over a third of alerts are legitimate transactions
✕ Average 45–90 minutes per case — 3 analysts handling 200+ alerts/day
✕ No cross-signal correlation between transaction patterns and customer behaviour
✕ Inconsistent decisions — outcome depends on analyst experience and fatigue
✕ No real-time governance, no audit trail, no explainability
✕ Reactive compliance — 15% of STR filing deadlines missed
As-Is Process: Manual fraud investigation with 4 actor swim lanes, sequential handoffs, and bottlenecks
Section 02
To-Be Process — Proposed State
AI-powered multi-agent fraud investigation with governance
Proposed State

A governed multi-agent AI pipeline that automates fraud investigation with explainable decisions, human oversight for high-risk cases, and real-time regulatory compliance.

1. INGEST — Fraud Alert & Orchestrator
Fraud alert from rule engine triggers Orchestrator. Validates, classifies urgency, routes to agents, logs, and enforces SLA. Guardrails layer applies PII masking, schema validation, hallucination check.
2. AGENTS — 4-Agent Pipeline
Agent 1: Transaction (risk_score 0–100) → Agent 2: Customer (anomaly_score 0–100) → Agent 3: Risk & Policy (composite_risk 0–100) → Agent 4: Recommendation (decision + actions[]).
3. Conditional Check & Decision Routing
Combined risk > 70 → priority routing. Decision Type: APPROVE → Auto-Approve (low risk, proceeds). HOLD/BLOCK → routed to HITL Review.
4. ROUTING — Human-in-the-Loop Review
Fraud Investigator reviews AI recommendation. Options: Approve / Override / Escalate / Request Info. Override → Escalation Path to Senior Manager / Compliance with STR/SAR filing.
5. OUTCOME — with Full Audit Trail
APPROVED (transaction proceeds) | HELD & VERIFIED (after human review) | BLOCKED & REPORTED (STR filed + frozen). Every agent output, routing decision, timestamp, and human action logged with full traceability.
✓ False positive rate reduced from 35% to ~15% through multi-signal correlation
✓ AI resolution in ~3 seconds (97% faster) + targeted HITL only when needed
✓ Cross-agent correlation of transaction, customer, and policy signals
✓ Consistent, explainable decisions with confidence scores and evidence
✓ Real-time guardrails mapped to NIST AI RMF — 8 active controls
✓ Proactive compliance — regulatory flags raised during investigation
To-Be Process: Governed multi-agent AI pipeline with autonomous (A), human-in-the-loop (H), and escalation (E) activities

Structured Thinking
Root Cause Analysis & Stakeholder Mapping
5 Whys, assumption validation, and stakeholder needs assessment
5 Whys — Root Cause Analysis
#Why?Answer
1Why do banks lose money to fraud?Fraudulent transactions are approved before they are detected.
2Why are they not detected in time?Investigators cannot review cases fast enough — each case takes 45–90 minutes.
3Why does review take so long?Analysts must manually check 6–8 disconnected systems (core banking, AML, CRM, KYC, device logs, geolocation).
4Why are systems disconnected?Legacy infrastructure was built in silos; no unified investigation orchestration exists.
5Why has no unified system been built?Traditional rule-based engines can flag transactions but cannot reason, synthesize evidence, or make contextual recommendations — that requires agentic AI.

STOIC Framework
Prompt Engineering — 3 Iterations
Situation · Task · Objective · Instructions · Constraints
Iteration 0 — Naive
S — I need to detect fraud in banking. T — Build an AI system. O — Catch fraudulent transactions. I — Use machine learning. C — Must be accurate.
Vague, no domain specificity, no measurable outcomes. Produces generic responses.
Iteration 1 — Refined
S — Indian banks face rising UPI/NEFT/RTGS fraud. Manual investigation: 45-90 min/case. T — Design multi-agent AI pipeline. O — <5 min resolution, >90% accuracy, regulatory compliance. I — Specialized agents for transaction, behaviour, risk, recommendation. HITL for high-risk. C — Open-weight models. RBI/PMLA/FATF compliant. Auditable output.
Domain-specific, measurable targets, architectural direction.
Iteration 2 — Final
S — Mid-size bank: 2M+ txn/day, 3-person team, 200 cases, 35% false positives, 15% missed STR deadlines. T — 4-agent pipeline with conditional routing + HITL + structured output. O — 5 KPIs: >92% accuracy, FP <15%, <3 min AI, 100% STR, 100% schema. I — 4 named agents with specific signals, hallucination self-check, composite scoring. C — 8 constraints: 3 open-weight models, PII masking, SLA <30s, RBAC, n8n orchestration.

Why Multi-Agent Wins
vs. Rule Engine: Rules cannot reason about context (e.g., "elderly + new device + crypto = exploitation"), only match thresholds.
vs. Single ML: A single model cannot explain decisions in natural language or apply different regulatory frameworks.
vs. Single LLM: One model doing everything produces lower-quality outputs than specialized agents. Domain decomposition mirrors real fraud teams.
vs. Full Autonomous: RBI and FATF mandate human oversight for blocking decisions. Fully autonomous faces legal and ethical barriers.
Market Research Insights
₹14,483 Cr fraud losses in FY2023-24 (RBI Annual Report)
~2% of global financial crime flows detected (Interpol via McKinsey)
200–2,000% productivity gains with agentic AI vs. 15–20% traditional AI (McKinsey)
"Pilot Purgatory" — banks have AI models that fail when integrated. Gap is orchestration, not intelligence.
Regulatory Push — RBI AML/KYC + FATF pushing banks toward structured audit trails, not just risk scores.
Section 04
Agent Deep Dive
4 specialised agents with distinct analysis responsibilities
Transaction Analysis Agent

Analyses transaction characteristics against historical patterns and risk indicators.

Scoring Factors:
  • Amount deviation from customer average
  • Time-of-day risk (late night = higher)
  • Device fingerprint mismatch
  • Geo-location anomaly / VPN detection
  • Recipient risk (new, crypto, foreign)
  • Rule trigger severity weighting
Output: Risk Score 0–100 + findings list
Customer Behaviour Agent

Evaluates customer profile, behavioural patterns, and account anomalies.

Analysis Signals:
  • Login time/location anomalies
  • Recent password or device changes
  • Account maturity trust calculation
  • Elderly/vulnerable customer flags (age > 60)
  • Spending velocity vs. baseline
  • Session behaviour patterns
Output: Anomaly Score 0–100 + findings list
Risk & Policy Agent

Evaluates case against 6 bank policies and regulatory requirements.

Policies Checked:
  • POL-001: Enhanced due diligence (₹2L+ threshold)
  • POL-002: CTR filing (₹10L+ cash transactions)
  • POL-010: Combined risk threshold breach
  • POL-015: Crypto platform transfers
  • POL-020: Cross-border / VPN detection
  • POL-025: Elderly customer protection
  • POL-030: New beneficiary + high value
Output: Policy Action + violations + regulatory flags
Recommendation Agent

Synthesises all agent outputs into a final actionable recommendation.

Synthesis Output:
  • Final decision with confidence %
  • Urgency classification (LOW→CRITICAL)
  • Ordered recommended actions
  • Evidence summary with all scores
  • Hallucination check flags
  • Human-readable explanation
Output: Decision + Confidence + Actions

Time: Normal hours · Device: Known

CASE-2024-002: Ambiguous Pattern
HIGH RISK
Customer: Priya Sharma (ID: CUST-4521)
Age: 32 · Account: 3 years · Risk Profile: Low
Transaction: INR 2,50,000 · IMPS
To: Crypto exchange · From: Delhi (VPN detected)
Time: 2:30 AM · Device: New device
Rule Triggers: Large transfer, high-risk destination, unusual time, new device, VPN
Expected Outcome: Hold & Verify
Key Signals: Multiple red flags but young account with no prior fraud. Late-night crypto transfer via VPN warrants investigation.
CASE-2024-003: High-Risk / Potential ATO
CRITICAL
Customer: Meera Devi (ID: CUST-7712)
Age: 68 · Account: 15 years · Risk Profile: Low
Transaction: INR 5,00,000 · RTGS
To: Unknown entity · From: Foreign IP (Nigeria)
Time: 3:45 AM · Device: Unknown device
Rule Triggers: Elderly customer, large transfer, foreign origin, new device, password change, rapid succession
Expected Outcome: Block & Escalate immediately
Key Signals: Classic account takeover pattern. Elderly customer, sudden password change, unknown device from foreign IP, large amount to unknown recipient.
